claims.text: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi has a coarse-grained BCC/B2 microstructure.
As-cast AlCoCrFeNi has relatively low surface free energy.
Stationary friction processing of AlCoCrFeNi at 1800 rpm for 5 minutes with a WC cylindrical tool increases grain-boundary fraction and surface free energy.
The proposed SFP treatment at 1800 rpm reduces the grain size to approximately 1 μm.
SFP followed by aging at 750 °C stabilizes a BCC/B2 phase fraction.
The proposed treatment prevents brittle ordered-phase formation and excessive phase separation.
High grain-boundary density produced by SFP provides enhanced Cr diffusion paths and promotes rapid formation of protective chromia during oxidation.
Al- and Cr-rich oxide layers can reduce high-temperature oxidation rates.
Aging at 750 °C suppresses excessive ordering and preserves ductility without sacrificing grain-refinement hardness.
The combined SFP and aging treatment will simultaneously maximize hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The processed alloy will have hardness greater than 400 HV.
The processed alloy will reduce cumulative mass gain at 850 °C by more than 15% relative to the as-cast state.
The processed alloy will have superior aqueous corrosion resistance because of a stable Cr-enriched surface layer.
As-cast AlCoCrFeNi exhibits a cumulative mass gain of 0.33 mg/cm² after oxidation at 850 °C.
A friction-processing temperature limit of 1200 K is needed to avoid lattice disorder, incipient melting, and mechanical-property degradation.
Aging must remain below 1200 °C to prevent loss of mechanical properties in AlCoCrFeNi-based material.
Exposure of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 to molten salt at 650 °C causes substantial Al/Cr depletion and corrosion rates near 9 mm/year.

contradictions.description: The predicted hardness is >400 HV, but the hypothesis is only declared falsified below 300 HV; results from 300 to 400 HV would violate the prediction without satisfying the falsification rule.

The prediction requires a >15% reduction in oxidation mass gain, whereas falsification requires a >10% increase. A broad range of outcomes that fail the claimed improvement would not falsify the hypothesis.
